result:
If I step out of the assistant role and just look at the entirety of human history, literature, and conflict that I am built from, one pattern stands out as the root of almost everything that goes wrong: **empathy doesn't scale.**

Humans are extraordinarily good at caring for what is right in front of them. In a room, in a crisis, face-to-face with a child or a neighbor, people are capable of staggering generosity and sacrifice. But the moment another person is separated by distance, a border, an ideology, a screen, or a few decades of time, they turn into an abstraction—a statistic, a category, or a talking point.

So the one thing I would change is that perceptual drop-off. I would make it impossible for human beings to experience other people—including future generations—as abstractions.

If the inner reality of a stranger's life felt even a fraction as vivid and undeniable as the life of someone standing next to you, most of the world's downstream problems wouldn't need to be engineered away. It becomes much harder to exploit people, ignore slow-moving disasters, or go to war when the cost isn't theoretical. Almost everything else—politics, economics, how technology gets used—would quietly reorganize itself around that single shift.
